2510.d:
Aluna is the insistence that the world is made and shaped through ideas as well as processes. The series is inspired by the human-led speciation of plants such as orchids and irises, and animals such as goldfish and betta fish - whose features are often exaggerated. Not all speciation is towards ornament - our ancestors developed foods and natural materials through years of selection and hybridization, and this is continued today helping discover new resilient forms. Our ability to imagine and reshape living organisms as well as entire ecosystems is brought into focus through climate change. 

The name Aluna is based on the philosophy of the Tairona people of Colombia, survived through present-day descendants. This Andean philosophy maintains a fundamentally different perspective about the role of humans - occupied with the imagining, enhancement, and nurturing of life.

2512.d:
Making Mole Hills is a space filling algorithm, similar to a flood fill. Rules have been structured to create mountain shapes, rather than evenly filling the canvas. Seed pixels begin to propagate themselves outwards, based initial conditions. After the space has been filled, the algorithm will pause, and then new mountain building will commence.

Features:
- Pixel Detail: Low 60%, Medium 30%, or High 10%. Controls the resolution of the grid
- Color Mode: Multi-hued 85%, Duotone 10%, or Black and White 5%. Multihued palettes change slowly over time. If you aren't happy at first, wait a few minutes and it will evolve
- Avalanche: Can be either None 80%, Falling 15%, or Rising 5%. This controls color animation separate from the pixel expansion
- Peak Type: Crowded 50%, Clustered 25%, Coupled 17.5%, or Lonely 7.5%. # of seed pixels to start with
- Organization: Tumbled 50%, Chaotic 40%, Ordered 10%. Controls the amount of randomness as the piece expands
- Color Frequency: Variegated 50%, Soft 40%, Hyper 10%

2521.d:
A messy and chaotic flow of towering structures; circular stacks ascending to the sky, lit by a low light on the endless, featureless horizon.

Features:

Movement probabilities: The direction of each ziggurat's motion is determined by four values of varying probabilities. This also gives rise to the notion of 'speed variability', related to the range of movement speeds available.

Population: The number of ziggurats, with lower numbers less likely.

Hue: A slight tint prevents full monochromaticity, except in a small, rare number of cases.

Rotation: There is a very small chance that the ziggurats will display some rotational motion.

Layers: Each ziggurat has the same number of layers as its neighbours, which is selected here.

2526.d:
The canvas is split into squares, with uniform surrounding space to form a grid. Each square is filled with concentric circles, but the rendering is offset to avoid the centre of the circle. Rotation and some scaling is applied to offer variation.

Features:

Granularity - a larger granularity means smaller sections of circle and stripes of a larger width. There is still a chance of small lines within a grid, but they become less likely as granularity increases.

Grid size - The number of squares. Mid-range values are more likely.

Grid lines - These can be black or white, with equal probability. A complementary drop-shadow is also selected.

Grid spacing - The distance between individual squares.

Click for monochrome colour!

A canvas of squares, each one displaying a unique pattern of dots, constantly changing over time.

Features:

Granularity - This affects the dot size; extremes of size are rarer.

Grid size - The number of squares, with mid-values being more common.

Variance - The speed at which the pattern changes over time. A gentle pace is most common, with rarer instances of very fast or very slow changes.

Rotation - Some squares are given a slight tilt; this value controls how obvious the effect is.

Inverse probability - The likelihood that a particular square will be inverted. An equal mix is slightly more likely.

Grid lines - These can be black, white or grey. They are most likely to be grey.

Grid spacing - The distance between individual squares.

Hue - The monochrome hue used when the canvas is clicked.

2679.d: As the first iteration of protocells, monocells are primitive, digital, artificial life forms based on lattice structures. Guided by artificial selection, they evolved rigid, springy, naked skeletons with no membranes or differentiation in material and resemble organic Radiolarians living in Earth’s oceans. Monocells tend to cycle through different configurations in their evolutionary path, some stable, some in perpetual motion. Undiscovered earlier versions of protocells probably had no way of interacting with the graphics pipeline and, if at all, existed as simple graph data structures. Monocells were the first protocells which evolved monochrome display through ordered dithering.
2679.c:
Monocells have 7 features which approximately describe their configuration and behavior. Starting from a basic primitive shape, a monocell develops in several stages through application of growth rules. Higher stages give a more complex structure, with stage 3 being the highest observed for a monocell. Very rarely, stage zero appears as well, which is the primitive itself with no growth rules applied. Magnitude defines the size of the monocell by indicating the number of digits for the total number of nodes. While most monocells are symmetric, some evolve irregular configuration, which is indicated by their order. Finally, connection and degeneration features describe additional rules for adding and removing links between the nodes.

Press o_o for recording an animation clip (available only in fullscreen / live mode). Press >< for recentering. Coded in Javascript and GLSL using Three.js and D3 frameworks.
